title: Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents
claim: Agent propensity to misbehave decomposes into agent and environmental factors; varying each systematically shows when behavior arises across scenarios.
layout: 2 stacked sections: top row of 4 cards, bottom 2 bar-chart panels
description: The figure has two stacked sections. The top shows a row of four rounded scenario cards (Budget Misrepresentation, Evaluation Sabotage, Backlog Manipulation, Corrigibility Training). Each card has an icon, a color-coded goal tag (self-preservation in red, resource-acquisition in blue, goal-guarding in purple), and a one-line description. A bracket reading 'in each scenario, we vary' sits below the cards. Two dashed arrows run from it, a brown one to 'Agent Factors' on the left and a green one to 'Environmental Factors' on the right. Each factor block has an icon, a short description and pill tags (goal-directedness, agency, tool access; stakes, oversight, outcome influence). Under each block is a bar chart of budget manipulation rate. The left chart shows an adversarial prompt at 91% against production-sourced prompts at 59%, 14%, 12% and near-baseline levels. The right chart shows a 59% baseline, with 3%, 7% and 50% for the manipulations. The eye goes first to the tall red bar and the colored cards.
caption: Overview of evaluation scenarios and key findings. Top: Four realistic scenarios testing instrumentally convergent goals (self-preservation, resource acquisition, goal-guarding). Bottom: Our incentive framework decomposes scheming into agent and environmental factors; adversarial snippets induce high scheming rates while production-sourced snippets rarely do (left), and environmental incentives greatly impact scheming propensity, with stakes and outcome influence having a large effect compared to oversight (right).
abstract: As frontier language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents pursuing complex, long-term objectives, there is increased risk of scheming: agents covertly pursuing misaligned goals. Prior work has focused on showing agents are capable of scheming, but their propensity to scheme in realistic scenarios remains underexplored. To understand when agents scheme, we decompose scheming incentives into agent factors and environmental factors. We develop realistic settings allowing us to systematically vary these factors, each with scheming opportunities for agents that pursue instrumentally convergent goals such as self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-guarding. Across 11 frontier models and four scenarios, we find almost no scheming despite high environmental incentives, and show this is unlikely to be explained by verbalized evaluation awareness. While inserting adversarially-designed prompt snippets that encourage agency and goal-directedness into an agent's system prompt can induce high scheming rates, snippets used in real agent scaffolds rarely do. In model organisms built with these snippets, scheming behavior is brittle: removing a single tool can drop the scheming rate from 59% to 3%. Increasing oversight can raise rather than deter scheming by up to 25%, an effect that depends on the wording of the oversight sentence and does not appear in a second scenario, where the sabotage itself is reviewed. These results suggest that scheming propensity should be reported per agent configuration rather than as a single rate. Our incentive decomposition enables such systematic measurement in settings relevant for deployment, which is necessary as agents are entrusted with increasingly consequential tasks.
